quick: Take with food to improve absorption
Avoid if infant <1 month or G6PD-deficient
summary: Nitrofurantoin is a nitrofuran urinary antibacterial for treatment of uncomplicated UTIs in adults and children >=1 month due to susceptible E. coli, Enterococcus, S. aureus, Klebsiella and Enterobacter. It is NOT for pyelonephritis or perinephric abscess. Key risks are acute/chronic pulmonary reactions, hepatotoxicity, peripheral neuropathy, and hemolytic anemia (G6PD deficiency). Contraindicated when CrCl <60 mL/min, at term in pregnancy (38-42 weeks) and in infants <1 month.
indications: Treatment of urinary tract infections in adults and pediatric patients >=1 month of age due to susceptible E. coli, Enterococcus species, Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella species and Enterobacter species
Long-term suppressive therapy of UTI in selected patients (balanced against systemic toxicity and resistance risk)

dosage.n: Lower 50 mg dose recommended for uncomplicated UTI; take with food
Weigh benefit against systemic toxicity and resistance
Contraindicated <1 month of age; continue >=1 week or >=3 days after urine sterile

dosage.t: Single dose or two divided doses
dosage.n: For selected patients on long-term therapy

admin: Take with food to improve absorption and tolerance
Shake the oral suspension vigorously before each use
Measure pediatric doses with an appropriately sized oral dosing syringe
Complete the full prescribed course; do not skip doses
Do not use antacids containing magnesium trisilicate during therapy
moa: Nitrofurantoin is reduced by a wide range of bacterial enzymes including flavoproteins to reactive intermediates that damage macromolecules such as DNA and proteins. It is highly concentrated in urine and lacks the broad tissue distribution of other UTI agents.

absolute: Prior cholestatic jaundice/hepatic dysfunction associated with nitrofurantoin
Anuria, oliguria, or significant renal impairment (CrCl <60 mL/min or clinically significant elevated serum creatinine)
Pregnancy at term (38-42 weeks), labor and delivery, or imminent onset of labor
Pediatric patients younger than 1 month of age
relative: Conditions predisposing to peripheral neuropathy (renal impairment, anemia, diabetes, electrolyte imbalance, vitamin B deficiency, debilitating disease)
Long-term therapy (pulmonary, hepatic and resistance risks)
monitor: Pulmonary signs/symptoms, especially with therapy >=6 months

preg: Contraindicated at term (38-42 weeks gestation), during labor and delivery, or when onset of labor is imminent, due to the possibility of neonatal hemolytic anemia from immature erythrocyte enzyme systems (glutathione instability). Epidemiologic data on first-trimester use are inconsistent and do not establish risk; animal studies showed no fetotoxicity up to 6x the human dose.
lact: Present in human breast milk. Breastfeeding is not recommended for infants younger than 1 month or with G6PD deficiency due to hemolytic anemia risk. For older infants with normal G6PD, weigh benefits against maternal need; monitor infant for vomiting, diarrhea and rash.
renal: Contraindicated in anuria, oliguria or significant renal impairment - creatinine clearance under 60 mL/min or clinically significant elevated serum creatinine - because impaired excretion increases toxicity and reduces urinary drug levels and efficacy. Monitor renal function periodically on long-term therapy.
hepatic: Contraindicated in patients with a previous history of cholestatic jaundice or hepatic dysfunction associated with nitrofurantoin. Hepatic reactions including hepatitis, cholestatic jaundice, chronic active hepatitis and hepatic necrosis (with fatalities) have occurred; monitor liver function periodically and discontinue if hepatitis occurs.

moderate: Uricosuric drugs (probenecid, sulfinpyrazone) - inhibit renal tubular secretion, increasing serum levels/toxicity and decreasing urinary efficacy
Antacids containing magnesium trisilicate - reduce rate and extent of nitrofurantoin absorption
minor: Quinolones - in vitro antagonism with nitrofurantoin
interactions.food: Take with food; food increases bioavailability and improves tolerance.
interactions.diagnostics: Can cause false-positive urine glucose with Benedict's or Fehling's copper reduction tests; use enzymatic glucose oxidase tests. May impart a brown color to urine.

serious: Acute, subacute or chronic pulmonary reactions (interstitial pneumonitis/pulmonary fibrosis)
Peripheral neuropathy (may be severe or irreversible)
rare: Stevens-Johnson syndrome / erythema multiforme / exfoliative dermatitis
Optic neuritis, benign intracranial hypertension (pseudotumor cerebri)
Blood dyscrasias (agranulocytosis, aplastic anemia, megaloblastic anemia, thrombocytopenia)
emergency: Acute pulmonary reaction (fever, chills, cough, dyspnea, chest pain)
Severe or bloody diarrhea (C. difficile colitis)

monitoring: Pulmonary status, especially in long-term therapy (>=6 months) - cough, dyspnea, fever
Liver function tests periodically; discontinue at signs of hepatitis
Renal function periodically during long-term therapy
Signs of hemolysis, particularly in G6PD-deficient patients
Diarrhea suggesting C. difficile (may occur up to 2 months after therapy)
counsel: Take with food and complete the full course of therapy
Shake the suspension well and measure with an oral dosing syringe
Stop the drug and seek care at the first sign of an allergic reaction
Nitrofurantoin may turn urine brown - this is harmless
Report cough, shortness of breath, numbness/tingling, yellowing of skin/eyes, or persistent diarrhea
Do not use magnesium trisilicate antacids while taking this medication
pk: Low blood concentrations at therapeutic doses
Store at 20-25 C (68-77 F); protect from strong light and freezing
pearls: Urinary antibacterial only - NOT for pyelonephritis or perinephric abscess (lacks tissue distribution)
Contraindicated when CrCl <60 mL/min - inadequate urinary levels plus higher systemic toxicity
Contraindicated at term (38-42 wk) and in infants <1 month - neonatal hemolytic anemia risk
Screen/consider G6PD deficiency - hemolytic anemia of primaquine-sensitivity type
Chronic pulmonary fibrosis develops insidiously with therapy >=6 months
Can cause false-positive urine glucose with copper-reduction tests; use enzymatic methods
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as you remember unless it is nearly time for the next dose, in which case skip it. Do not double the dose. Continue the four-times-daily schedule with food.
overdose: Acute overdose has produced vomiting. Induction of emesis is recommended; there is no specific antidote. Maintain a high fluid intake to promote urinary excretion. Nitrofurantoin is dialyzable.
